Hormuz Adds a Cloud Clause

Iran wants its control of Hormuz to outlast the war and pay off afterward. Shipping would come with charges for security, insurance and environmental protection. Tehran’s armed gatekeeper has plans for a service desk. 

On Oct. 11, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Washington had accepted some of Iran’s seven conditions for reopening the strait, while its answers on the rest remained unclear. “We consider their response insufficient,” he said. The concessions rest on Rezaei’s word. 

Washington approached Tehran through Pakistan, Qatar and Iraq, according to Rezaei. The channels are diplomatic. His warning reaches into the region’s technology infrastructure. 

“If war breaks out again, many of the cables, data centers and artificial intelligence centers” would come within range, he said. Rezaei valued those assets at more than $2 trillion without identifying specific facilities or explaining the estimate. 

Gulf states hosting expensive American and European technology have acquired a place in Iran’s bargaining strategy. 

American military power has failed to produce an uncontested passage. Iran proposes to turn contested passage into income and threatens infrastructure belonging to countries that host somebody else’s investment.

The shipping rules are still under negotiation. The cloud has already received a missile warning.

🎙 Exclusive | Iran's ambassador rejects allegations of Tehran’s role in British airbase incident

📌 London, IRNA - Iran’s Ambassador to the United Kingdom, Seyyed Ali Mousavi, has categorically rejected allegations regarding Tehran’s role in the incident at the Fairford military base and urged the British government to refrain from making unfounded accusations.

During a meeting on Monday with Stephen Doughty, the UK’s Minister of State for the Middle East, at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, Mousavi reiterated that Iran had no involvement whatsoever in the matter and called on London to present any evidence it claims to possess.
​
Mousavi stressed the need to avoid unsubstantiated accusations, recalling that the Islamic Republic had previously urged the British government to refrain from hasty positions and unproven claims against Tehran.
​
He also reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to cooperate with relevant institutions in both countries within the framework of an investigation into the incident, noting that Tehran had already expressed this willingness.
​
The ambassador underscored Iran’s commitment to its international obligations under international law, stating that all countries must adhere to their international commitments, including respect for national sovereignty, the principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of others, and the prohibition of military aggression.
​
The meeting comes amid recent claims by British officials regarding Iran’s alleged role in the Fairford case. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday repeated previous allegations in the House of Commons without providing public evidence and announced further sanctions against the Islamic Republic of Iran.
​
According to reports, the UK’s Counter-Terrorism Police investigation into the Sept. 27 incident is ongoing, and all seven individuals arrested in connection with the case have been released on bail.
​
UK counter-terrorism police had also previously confirmed that no improvised explosive devices were found during their examination of vehicles linked to the incident.
